# Brief: write up why the number two joint failed, for the review on Friday

The number two joint wept at the eleven o'clock position eighteen days after it
was closed. It has been opened, the face has been checked and is out of flat,
and the joint has been remade. Nobody is in any doubt about what to do next time
on that particular joint. What we do not have is a written account that would
stop this happening on a different joint, and that is what Friday's review needs.

## What we know

The joint was closed on the third by the evening crew. The job record is thin
but not absent: it names the crew, the gasket lot, and a single final value for
the fasteners. It does not record a pattern and it does not record passes.

The face was machined during the same outage. It passed the flatness check after
machining, and the check sheet is in the folder with a legible signature on it,
so the face was flat when it went together.

The joint sealed on first pressurisation and held through the hydrostatic. It
was in service for eighteen days. The weep started small and was found on a
routine walk-down, so we have no idea exactly when it began.

On strip-down the face was out of flat by roughly twice the allowable, with the
high region opposite the eleven o'clock position. The gasket showed a clear
witness of uneven compression consistent with that.

## What I think happened and what I want you to check

I think the fasteners were pulled up to final value in one pass, going around
the circle. It would explain the shape — the face takes a set from wherever the
pull started, and the region opposite it is left high — and it would explain why
the joint sealed and tested fine, since the gasket is compliant enough to hide
the set until it relaxes.

It is a theory, and the review will treat it as fact if we present it as one, so
please do the work to make it more than that:

- Talk to the evening crew. Not to blame them — the record says nobody told them
  otherwise, and the standing instruction sheet in the shop does not mention
  passes or a crossing sequence at all. Find out what they actually did.
- Pull the last two years of joint failures on this class of vessel and see how
  many have this signature: sealed, tested, wept between two and six weeks, face
  out of flat opposite the weep. My recollection is that there are three. If
  there are three, that is a pattern and Friday has a real finding.
- Check whether the jobs that did not fail have anything in their records that
  the failures do not. If the surviving records mention a crossing sequence and
  the failed ones do not, that is the whole argument and it makes itself.

## The recommendation I expect this to land on

That the tightening procedure gets written down as a procedure rather than
living in whichever fitter happens to be on shift: crossing sequence, several
passes, values recorded per pass, and the pattern recorded rather than assumed.
And that the job record grows the fields to hold it, because a procedure that
has nowhere to be recorded is a procedure that is only followed when somebody is
watching.

If the evidence does not support that, say so. A review that adopts a procedure
on a theory and then sees the failures continue is worse off than one that says
the cause is still open.

## Format

Two pages. First page: what happened, what the evidence says, what the cause
was. Second page: what changes, who owns each change, and how we would know in
six months whether it worked. Do not write a timeline longer than the analysis —
the last three of these were mostly timeline and the review spent its hour
reading it.

Circulate by Thursday noon so people arrive having read it.

## What not to put in it

Do not put a root-cause diagram in it. The last two reviews spent twenty minutes
arguing with the boxes on the diagram instead of with the finding, and the boxes
are not where the argument belongs.

Do not name the evening crew in the written version. Name them to me if you need
to, but a document that circulates with two names in it turns a procedural
finding into a personnel matter and the procedural finding is the one that stops
this happening again. The standing instruction sheet is the thing at fault here
and it has no feelings about being named.

Do not recommend more inspection. It is the recommendation every one of these
lands on when the cause is genuinely unclear, and the cause here is not unclear.
More inspection on a joint that seals and tests correctly finds nothing, and it
costs an outage day each time.
